people/duns-scotus/summary: Scottish Franciscan, the 'Subtle Doctor', who taught at Oxford, Paris and Cologne. He argued for the univocity of being, the primacy of will and love, and the Immaculate Conception of Mary through 'preservative redemption' — a view defined as dogma in 1854.
people/william-of-ockham/summary: English Franciscan whose nominalism denied the real existence of universals and stressed God's absolute power. Summoned to Avignon, he sided with the Franciscan Spirituals on poverty against John XXII and fled to the emperor in Munich. His 'razor' and covenantal theology influenced late medieval thought and young Luther's teachers.
people/william-of-ockham/keyIdeas/1: Absolute and ordained power of God
people/gregory-palamas/summary: Athonite monk and archbishop of Thessalonica who defended hesychast prayer against Barlaam, distinguishing God's unknowable essence from his uncreated energies in which believers truly participate. Councils of 1341–1351 upheld his teaching; he was canonised in 1368.
people/sergius-of-radonezh/summary: Hermit who founded the Holy Trinity monastery north-east of Moscow and introduced cenobitic life in Russia. Humble, peacemaking and revered as a wonderworker, he blessed Prince Dmitri before Kulikovo (1380) and inspired a wave of northern monastic foundations.
people/john-wycliffe/summary: Oxford philosopher and priest who argued that Scripture is the supreme authority, that the true church is the elect, and that a corrupt clergy forfeits its authority. He rejected transubstantiation and inspired the first complete English Bible. Condemned posthumously at Constance, he is called 'the Morning Star of the Reformation'.
people/julian-of-norwich/summary: English anchoress who, after sixteen visions during severe illness in 1373, wrote Revelations of Divine Love — the first book in English known to be written by a woman. She speaks of God's love, Christ as mother and the hope that 'all shall be well'.
people/catherine-of-siena/summary: Dominican tertiary and mystic who, though largely unschooled, dictated The Dialogue and hundreds of letters to popes and rulers. She urged Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome and worked for church unity during the Western Schism. Declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970.
people/jan-hus/summary: Czech preacher at Prague's Bethlehem Chapel and rector of the university, influenced by Wycliffe. He criticised indulgences and clerical corruption and defined the church as the community of the predestined. Summoned to Constance under safe-conduct, he was burned on 6 July 1415, sparking the Hussite movement.
people/jan-hus/keyIdeas/0: Christ, not the pope, as head of the church
people/jan-hus/keyIdeas/2: Communion in both kinds (taken up by followers)
people/afonso-i-of-kongo/name: Afonso I of Kongo (Mvemba a Nzinga)
people/afonso-i-of-kongo/summary: King of Kongo from 1509 who made Catholicism the religion of his court, studied the Scriptures and canon law, and sent his son Henrique to Lisbon and Rome to become a bishop. His letters to King João III protested Portuguese slave-trading that was depopulating his kingdom.
people/erasmus/summary: Dutch humanist, the most famous scholar of his day, whose Greek New Testament (1516) and editions of the Fathers fuelled the call 'back to the sources'. He satirised clerical abuses in The Praise of Folly but stayed Catholic, debating Luther on free will (1524–25).
people/erasmus/keyIdeas/1: Return to biblical and patristic sources
people/bartolome-de-las-casas/summary: Spanish colonist and encomendero who, convicted by preaching on Sirach 34, freed his Indigenous labourers, became a Dominican and spent fifty years denouncing the conquest's cruelties. Bishop of Chiapas, author of A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, he argued at Valladolid (1550) for Indigenous rights; he early proposed African slaves as substitutes, which he later repented.
people/bartolome-de-las-casas/keyIdeas/0: Indigenous peoples as rational and free
people/huldrych-zwingli/summary: Swiss humanist priest who, from 1519 at Zürich's Grossmünster, preached through the Bible and led the city's Reformation: abolishing the Mass, images and fasting rules. He taught a symbolic, memorial view of the Lord's Supper, broke with Luther at Marburg and died in battle at Kappel.
people/martin-luther/summary: Augustinian friar and Wittenberg professor whose protest against indulgences (1517) became the Protestant Reformation. He taught justification by grace through faith alone, the authority of Scripture over popes and councils and the priesthood of all believers, and translated the Bible into German. Excommunicated in 1521, he married Katharina von Bora and shaped Lutheran worship with hymns and catechisms; his late anti-Jewish writings are widely repudiated today.
people/thomas-muntzer/summary: An early follower of Luther who turned against him, preaching direct revelation of the Spirit, apocalyptic judgement on the ungodly and the rights of the common people. He led peasant forces at Frankenhausen and was executed in 1525.
people/thomas-cranmer/summary: Archbishop of Canterbury under Henry VIII and Edward VI who annulled Henry's marriage and shaped the English Reformation. His Books of Common Prayer (1549, 1552) and Forty-two Articles defined Anglican worship and doctrine. Under Mary I he recanted, then withdrew his recantations and was burned at Oxford.
people/balthasar-hubmaier/summary: A doctor of theology and former Catholic preacher who became the most learned early Anabaptist, writing on believers' baptism and religious freedom (On Heretics and Those Who Burn Them). Unlike the Swiss Brethren he accepted the magistrate's sword. He was burned in Vienna in 1528.
people/ignatius-of-loyola/summary: Basque soldier converted while recovering from wounds (1521), who devised the Spiritual Exercises and founded the Society of Jesus (1540). The Jesuits became the leading force of Catholic renewal in education and global mission.
people/menno-simons/summary: Frisian priest who, disturbed by the Münster debacle in which his brother died, joined the peaceful Anabaptists in 1536. As itinerant elder with a price on his head he gathered scattered congregations; his followers became known as Mennonites.
people/philip-melanchthon/summary: Humanist Greek professor at Wittenberg, Luther's closest colleague, who wrote the first Protestant systematic theology (Loci communes, 1521) and the Augsburg Confession (1530). Called 'Teacher of Germany' for his educational reforms; his irenic stance provoked later Lutheran disputes.
people/conrad-grebel/summary: Son of a Zürich patrician, a humanist student of Zwingli who broke with him over infant baptism and state control of reform. On 21 January 1525 he baptised George Blaurock, beginning the Anabaptist movement; he died of plague the following year.
people/heinrich-bullinger/summary: Zwingli's successor at Zürich for 44 years, the most widely read Reformed theologian of the 16th century. He wrote the Second Helvetic Confession (1566), the Decades of sermons and the Consensus Tigurinus with Calvin (1549); he developed covenant theology.
people/heinrich-bullinger/keyIdeas/1: Preaching of the Word is the Word of God
people/francis-xavier/summary: Navarrese co-founder of the Jesuits who sailed to Goa in 1542 and preached among the Parava pearl-fishers of south India, in the Moluccas and from 1549 in Japan. He died on Shangchuan Island off China awaiting entry. His tomb in Goa remains a pilgrimage site.
people/john-calvin/summary: French humanist lawyer converted to evangelical faith, who led the Reformation in Geneva from 1541. His Institutes of the Christian Religion and biblical commentaries systematised Reformed theology: God's sovereignty, union with Christ, double grace of justification and sanctification, spiritual real presence and predestination. Geneva trained pastors for France, Scotland and beyond; his role in Servetus's execution remains a lasting stain.
people/teresa-of-avila/summary: Spanish Carmelite nun of converso descent who founded the reformed Discalced Carmelites. Her Life, The Way of Perfection and The Interior Castle map the soul's journey through prayer to union with God. In 1970 she became the first woman declared a Doctor of the Church.
people/teresa-of-avila/keyIdeas/1: Mental prayer as friendship with God
people/theodore-beza/summary: French humanist who succeeded Calvin as leader of Geneva's church and academy. He edited the Greek New Testament, defended Huguenot resistance after St Bartholomew's Day, and systematised predestination in a more scholastic, supralapsarian direction.
